messages.body_plain:
Hi Sri,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. The script I uploaded a while ago was to generate seg files to be loaded into IGV for visualization. Basically it parses the combined CNV calls from all chromosomes in all samples into one text file for one sample. The code is only for demo — I am sure you can parse this very easily too. With this said, I think the tumorsample_lookup.txt contains all the tumor names so for each tumor sample, I searched for its called CNVs and save them as a text file for that specific sample.

Hope that this clarifies,
Yuchao

messages.subject: Unexpected output: A deletioon where no deletion should be.
messages.subject_clean: Unexpected output: A deletioon where no deletion should be.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Yuchao,

we noticed a little strange behaviour in CODEX and wanted to ask whether you could give us hints where to start investigating the problem.

Here is the setup: We sequenced 31 exomes from animals with conditional knockouts of p53. Since conditional, one particular organ is never affected. Those are the samples called "Normal" in the IGV screenshot.
As a confirmation, a matched knockout sample (from the same animal) is also included, named "Tumor 1".
Unexpectedly, the results from CODEX also show a deletion in the Normal 1 sample. This should not happen.
We tried to play around with Coverage cutoffs, but it did not help.

The corresponding lines from the Codex output:
chr11 del 69586841 69590768 3,928 5750 5756 11 356 0,062 306,77 282,493
chr11 del 69586841 69590768 3,928 5750 5756 31 561 0,111 440,259 415,982

The first line corresponds to the Tumor 1, the second line to the Normal 1. How can it happen, that IGV clearly shows the non-knockout in Normal 1, but CODEX reports a knockout?
The parameters where:
getcoverage - mapqcthresh = 20
qc - cov_thresh = c(20,6000)
qc - length_thresh = c(20,2000)
qc - mapp_thresh = 0.9
qc - gc_thresh = c(20,80)

Additionally, we have more matched Tumor samples, where no deletion is shown, also IGV confirms the deletion.
Is there a way to get the reason from CODEX, why a deletion is reported or not reported?
How should we proceed? What are good ways to look into the data and see what leads CODEX to its decision?

Best and thanks for your comment!
Jens

messages.subject_clean: Unexpected output: A deletioon where no deletion should be.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jens,

>From the CODEX final output, the number of observed reads in tumor1 is 11 (with expected reads Yhat 356) and the number of observed reads in normal1 is 31 (with expected reads Yhat 561). It seems to me from your IGV screenshot the number of reads for normal1 is way larger than 31. Maybe something is wrong with the index?

ref_qc tells you the start and end position of exonic targets after QC. You can use start(ref_qc) and end(ref_qc) to get the start and end positions for the targets. Maybe do a check on these see if the targets pass the QC?
Also check the corresponding Y_qc for normal1 in the exonic targets actually sum up to 31 and for tumor1 they sum up to 11.

Hope that this helps,
Yuchao

--
Yuchao Jiang (yuc...@mail.med.upenn.edu)
PhD student in Genomics and Computational Biology
University of Pennsylvania

First of all thank you! CODEX mostly seems to work great, and it's unique because it has a version adapted to analyze CNVs in targeted exome sequencing data. All of the other programs I have so far found are meant to be used for whole exome sequencing data only.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think I got the problem solved. I inspected the code more by going through step by step what is generated in different stages. The problem was really because of only one variant being called for the chromosome.

In

finalcall=finalcall[-1,]

the first row in finalcall matrix (containing the results) containing only NAs is removed. In the case of 0 or 2 or more variants, the matrix stays as matrix. But when only one variant would be called, this step changes the finalcall matrix into "value" for some reason. I solved this by forcing the matrix by adding

finalcall=(as.matrix(finalcall[-1,]))

which gives a matrix with rows and columns inverted, but I'm working on from here... Thanks for advice.

I'd still like to know if I have the permission to use this targeted exome sequencing analysis CODEX version in my master's thesis.

Best regards,
Salla

messages.subject: Re: Question about CODEX analysis
messages.subject_clean: Question about CODEX analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Noemie,

Thanks for your interest. Attached are the codes that we use internally to segment tumor genomes with paired normals. Note that if you use the default segment() function there isn’t too much difference based on our results.

If you samples come in an order of normal1, tumor1, normal2, tumor2, normal3, tumor3, …, then you need to use the command below:

N0 = dim(Y_qc)[1]
nsamp = length(sampname_qc)/2
relCN = matrix(0,N0,nsamp)
tumorid = 2*(1:nsamp)  % the indices of tumor samples normalid = tumorid -1  % the indices of normal samples

Also you need to install the package attached as well (don’t install directly from the CRAN, it’s not updated).

For your other questions, if you normalize tumor and normal separately, the signals in your tumor samples don’t have a benchmark to be compared to (as compared to if you normalize tumor with normal). Therefore, your signals (especially if they are recurrent in your tumor samples) will most likely be removed as a latent bias. To use the normalize2() function with argument of normal sample index, only biases in your normal samples will be removed by CODEX. I hope this answers your question.

Also you need to use the fractional mode for segmentation if your tumor samples are heterogeneous which is almost always the case for bulk sequencing.

Cheers,
Yuchao
